## Dynamical Systems Theory

Current psychiatric classification system largely rely on categorical models that treat mental disorders as distinct entities and define them based on symptom clusters. However, this system often fails to capture the fluid and fuzzy reality of clinical practice [@Joober2019]. The limitations of viewing psychiatric conditions as having fixed "essences" have prompted a shift toward Dynamical Systems Theory (DST), which conceptualizes psychopathology not as a fixed disease entity, but as a specific dynamical state of the brain and body [@Maj2005; @Kendler2015; @Joober2019].

This theory can be metaphorically envisioned as a high-dimensional state space, in which the vast array of neurobiological and psychosocial variables that define a person's mental state can be mapped onto distinct dimensions. Within this space, the mental state evolves along certain trajectories governed by the system's underlying rules of evolution. Rather than freely exploring the entire state space, these trajectories tend to converge toward stable orbits known as attractors, while the surrounding regions that pull the system toward a specific attractor are called a basin of attraction.

Neuroscience research has shown that this view of neural states as dynamical systems, in which network activity evolves toward stable configurations, has offered a principled account of persistent neural activity, working memory, and the computational properties of recurrent neural networks [@dominguez2007;@balaguer-ballester2018]. Analogously, psychiatric symptoms can be conceptualized as specific attractors within this landscape. While a healthy individual maintains the flexibility to transition between various attractors, a mental illness manifests when the system becomes trapped within deep, maladaptive basins that resist the transitions to other basins [@Salvi2021; @schefferEtAl2024a; @ngr2025].

## Neural Architecture as a Potential Energy Landscape

While the image of state space and attractor landscape provides a useful metaphor, the precise physical grounding in the brain's functional and structural organization remains a subject of ongoing investigation. It is increasingly hypothesized that the network structure of brain at variuos levels of organization shapes the geometry of the state space [@gu2018]. Within this framework, the matrix of synaptic weights ($W$) is thought to define a potential energy surface, or "energy landscape", where the altitudes represent the energy levels of neural activation [@watanabe2014].

Recent research on connectome harmonics and the eigenmodes of cortical traveling waves suggests that multi-scale structural connectivity provides a natural set of basis for brain dynamics [@atasoy2016; @abdelnour2018; @haggarty2025]. Connectome harmonics, which are calculated from the eigenmodes of the graph Laplacian derived from the connectome matrix, form the bases (dimensions) of the state space, thereby constraining the space in which neural systems can evolve. Spontaneous and task-evoked activity patterns can be expressed as trajectories within this specific geometry.

The synaptic weight matrix (W) shapes the spectrum of the Laplacian, thereby determining which eigenmodes are energetically favorable, how easily transitions between modes occur, and how stable particular configurations become [@delange2014]. In this sense, it can be understood that alterations in SC or FC reshape the eigen-spectrum, which in turn deforms the geometry of the attractor landscape. In other words, they define the low-dimensional manifold within which neural trajectories can unfold [@abdelnour2018]. Empirical studies using connectome spectral analysis in depression have shown that pathological states are associated with altered occupancy and energy distribution across harmonics, consistent with the alteration of the underlying state space [@atasoy2017].

As the system evolves according to its governing rules, it behaves like a ball rolling across a topography punctuated by a series of basins and ridges. Equilibrium points at the base of these valleys represent attractors, while peaks act as repellors that deflect the system toward neighboring basins. The "dynamic resilience" of a state is determined by the depth and steepness of these basins [@schefferEtAl2024a]; in a healthy, resilient system, sufficiently deep basins allow the brain to absorb perturbations and return efficiently to stable equilibria.

## Hysteresis and Network Rigidity

Hysteresis refers to the tendency for a system to remain trapped in a maladaptive state even after the initiating stressor has vanished. In a pathological state, intense local hyper-connectivity often develops resulting in deep, rigid basins, while healthy basins of attraction become degraded and shallow [@SvozCouche2017]. This "trapping" is rooted in multi-scale deficits that span from synaptic architecture to large-scale network dynamics.

At the synaptic level, this phenomenon is closely associated with impaired neuroplasticity and structural erosion, including decreased dendritic spine density, impaired long-term potentiation (LTP), and reduced expression of plasticity-related molecules such as Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF) [@Price2010; @Duman2012; @Kang2012; @Duman2016]. These cellular-level deficits translate into macroscopic abnormalities in large-scale functional networks, particularly the Default Mode Network (DMN) [@Yan2019; @Tozzi2021].

In healthy individuals, dynamic functional connectivity (DFC) exhibits significant flexibility, allowing the brain to transition seamlessly between a diverse repertoire of attractor states. In contrast, patients with depression exhibit reduced temporal variability and a restricted state repertoire. This network rigidity leads to excessive occupancy in sub-optimal states, most notably the depressive rumination associated with the hyper-segregated DMN [@Kaiser2016; @Demirta2016; @DOstilio2016; @Regonia2021; @Durstewitz2021; @An2024].

## Metastability: A Metric for Dynamical Flexibility

One way to formalize this flexibility more rigorously is through metastability. It indicates the capacity of the brain to fluctuate between multiple functional states [@deco2017]. Computational neuroscientists often quantify this property using the Kuramoto order parameter ($R(t)$), which measures the global level of synchronization across the brain at any given instant. Under complete independence, the phases of neural signals are uniformly distributed ($R \approx 0$), whereas full synchronization implies all phases are equal ($R \approx 1$). Metastability is defined as the variability of this synchronization over time, calculated as the standard deviation of the Kuramoto order parameter. High metastability indicates that the global synchronization level is constantly fluctuating, rather than remaining fixed.

This high metastability is interpreted as a hallmark of a healthy, adaptive system [@torres2024]. A brain with this property avoids being trapped in a state of fixed synchronization or a completely disordered state of incoherence. Instead, it maintains a dynamic balance between integration (synchronization) and segregation (desynchronization). This fluid regime ensures that the system does not settle permanently into a single attractor but retains the flexibility to rapidly reorganize and visit a diverse repertoire of functional configurations.

## Therapeutic Recovery as Landscape Remodeling

DST suggests that recovery requires remodeling the attractor landscape. Because pathological basins can be very deep and rigid, small perturbations often fail to dislodge the system. Intensive treatments, such as ECT and psychedelics, may provide enough energy to reset the system, and then allowing the system to settle into a new set of attractors (see Figure \@ref(fig:health_ECT)).

RElaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics (REBUS), which is one of the models of psychedelic action, integrates the "Entropic Brain" hypothesis with a predictive processing framework [@CarhartHarris2019]. The REBUS model postulates that psychedelics, through their $5\text{-HT}_{2\text{A}}$ agonism, induce a dysynchronization of higher-order cortical regions [@siegel2024]. This manifests as a relaxed precision-weighting on high-level prior beliefs, effectively decreasing the "stiffness" of the top-down cognitive constraints.

In a control-theoretic formulation, this acute perturbation was described as a "transient flattening of the control-energy landscape" [@Madsen2021; @Singleton2022]. Mechanistically, psychedelics lower the minimum energy required to transition between recurrent brain states, operationalized as a reduction in the energetic barriers separating diverse attractors. Energy-barrier reduction has been associated with shorter state dwell times and more entropic state sequences, consistent with enhanced exploration of the state space. Whether through the broad physiological reset of ECT or the desynchronization of psychedelics, the goal of these treatments remains consistent: to provide the system an opportunity to remodel the attractor landscape to healthy states [@Rao2018; @Rolls2020].
